title: Tail Latency and Request Fan-out
objectives: Explain why a request that fans out to many backends is slowed by their rare slow calls
Use hedged requests, deadlines and partial results to cut the tail
Estimate the share of slow requests from per-call odds and the fan-out width

cards.title: The slowest backend sets the pace
cards.body: A search or feed page often calls many backends in parallel and cannot answer until the last one replies. If each backend is slower than its own p99 on 1% of calls, independently, the chance that at least one of N calls is slow is 1 − 0.99^N: about 10% for 10 backends and about 63% for 100. At wide fan-out, a backend’s rare tail becomes the page’s normal case.

cards.title: Worked example: a page that fans out to 100 shards
cards.body: Assume: each shard answers in 10 ms at p50, 30 ms at p95 and 120 ms at p99; slow calls happen independently.
steps: Chance that all 100 shards are fast: 0.99^100 ≈ 0.366, so about 63% of pages wait for at least one call slower than 120 ms.
Hedge: if a shard has not replied by 30 ms (its p95), send the same read to another replica and take whichever answers first.

A call now stays slow only if both copies are slow. The copy starts 30 ms late, so it must answer within 90 ms; treating that as the same 1% tail gives roughly 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001 (a little more in practice, since 90 ms sits between the p95 and the p99).
Chance a page waits on a slow call: 1 − 0.9999^100 ≈ 1%, a few percent at worst, down from about 63%, for about 5% extra backend requests (only the calls past p95 get a copy).
cards.note: Hedging after the p95 trades a few percent more load for a large cut in the tail, but only for requests that are safe to send twice.

cards.title: A hedged read, step by step
cards.body: The client sends one copy, waits about the p95 latency, sends a second copy to another replica only if the first is still pending, and keeps the first answer.
steps: Send the read to replica A
Wait until about the p95 latency (30 ms)
Still no reply: send the same read to replica B
Use whichever reply arrives first
Cancel the other request

cards.title: What may be hedged, and how much
cards.body: Hedge only reads and other idempotent calls, or calls that carry an idempotency key. Wait for the p95 rather than sending two copies at once, which would double the load. Cap hedges with a budget (for example at most 5% extra requests) so that a slow cluster is not flooded with copies, and cancel the losing copy so it stops using the backend.

cards.title: Trap: tuning the average while pages hang
cards.body: A dashboard that shows only mean latency hides the problem. Track p99 and p99.9 for each fan-out level, give every call a deadline derived from the page budget, and where the product allows it return partial results (48 of 50 shards, marked partial) instead of waiting for the slowest shard.

questions.prompt: A page calls 100 backends in parallel. Each call is slower than its p99 on 1% of calls, independently. About what share of page loads wait for at least one slow call?

choices.label: About 1%
About 10%
About 37%
About 63%

questions.explanation: The page is fast only if all 100 calls are fast: 0.99^100 ≈ 0.37, so about 63% of pages hit a slow call. About 1% is the single-call rate, which ignores the fan-out. About 10% is the answer for 10 backends. About 37% is the share of pages with no slow call, not the share with one.

questions.prompt: When should a hedged copy of a read usually be sent?

choices.label: Immediately, alongside the first copy
Once the first copy passes about its p95 latency
Only after the first copy has returned an error code
After the first copy times out at 2 seconds

questions.explanation: Waiting for the p95 means only about 5% of calls get a copy, so the extra load is small. Sending both at once doubles the load. Waiting for an error or a 2-second timeout is a retry, which comes too late to help the tail.

questions.prompt: Which call is unsafe to hedge without extra protection?

choices.label: Reading a product’s price from a replica
Fetching one search shard’s top 10 results
Charging a card through a payment API
Loading a profile photo from a CDN

questions.explanation: Two copies of a charge can charge twice unless the call carries an idempotency key that the provider honours. The other three are reads: sending one twice costs load, not correctness.

questions.prompt: Each of 10 parallel backend calls is slow 1% of the time, independently. What percentage of requests hit at least one slow call?
assumptions: 10 independent calls per request
Each call is slow with probability 0.01
questions.explanation: Design implication: widening the fan-out from 10 to 100 calls takes this from about 10% to about 63%, so wide fan-out needs hedging, deadlines or partial results, not just faster averages.

questions.prompt: A search page must answer within 200 ms and fans out to 50 shards. At 180 ms two shards have not replied, and the product allows partial results. Best move?

choices.label: Wait for both shards, however long that takes
Return the 48 results, marked as partial
Fail the full page with a timeout error
Retry the two shards and wait for the retries

questions.explanation: Partial results keep the page inside its budget and lose little ranking quality. Waiting blows the budget, failing the page throws away 48 good answers, and a retry at 180 ms cannot finish in the 20 ms left.

questions.prompt: Order a hedged read.

items.label: Send the same read to replica B
Send the read to replica A
Cancel the slower request
Wait about the p95 latency
Use the first reply

questions.explanation: The copy goes out only after the p95 wait, and the loser is cancelled so it stops consuming backend capacity.

questions.prompt: A service hedges reads that pass their p95 latency. About how much extra backend load does that add?

choices.label: About 1%
About 5%
About 50%
About 100%

questions.explanation: Only calls slower than the p95, about 5% of them, get a second copy. 100% would be sending two copies of every call, 50% would be a trigger at the p50, and 1% a trigger at the p99.

flashcards.front: Why does fan-out make tails worse?
flashcards.back: A request waits for its slowest call; 1 − 0.99^N of requests hit a 1-in-100 slow call, about 63% at N = 100.
A second copy of a slow read sent to another replica after about the p95 wait; the first reply wins.
Reads and idempotent calls, under a budget such as 5% extra load.

sources.title: The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso, CACM 2013)

mechanism.title: How tail-tolerant fan-out works
steps: A front-end request is split into many backend calls, such as one per search shard or one per recommendation source, sent in parallel. The response is ready only when the slowest required call returns, so page latency is the maximum of N call latencies, not their average.

Rare slow calls come from ordinary causes: garbage-collection pauses, a noisy neighbour on the host, a cold cache, a compaction, a retransmitted packet. They are hard to remove one by one, so the design has to tolerate them instead.
The page budget (say 200 ms) is turned into per-call deadlines that leave time for merging and rendering. A call that misses its deadline is abandoned rather than waited on.

For reads, a hedged copy goes to a second replica once the first has waited about the p95. The first reply is used and the other request is cancelled. A budget caps the copies so that a slow cluster is not hit with twice the load.

Where the product allows it, the merger returns partial results and marks them, for example 48 of 50 shards. Search ranking and feeds degrade gracefully; payments and seat counts do not, so they are kept off wide fan-out paths.
Latency is monitored at p99 and p99.9 per fan-out level, because the average hides exactly the behaviour this design exists to fix.

useWhen: Search, feeds and recommendation pages that gather results from many shards or sources in parallel.
Read paths with replicas available, where a duplicate read costs only a little extra load.
Pages with a strict latency budget where an approximate or partial answer is better than a late one.
avoidWhen: Do not hedge non-idempotent writes such as payments or seat bookings unless every call carries an idempotency key.
Do not add hedging to a cluster that is already overloaded; the extra copies make the overload worse. Fix capacity or shed load first.
Do not return partial results where completeness is the requirement, such as a bank statement or an order total.

rows: A few percent more reads; reads only

numbers.title: From 63% slow pages to about 1%
assumptions: 100 shards per page
Per shard: p50 10 ms, p95 30 ms, p99 120 ms
Slow calls are independent
steps: Without hedging, the chance a page sees no slow call is 0.99^100 ≈ 0.366, so about 63% of pages wait more than 120 ms.
With a hedge at 30 ms, a call stays slow only if both copies are slow: about 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001, treating the copy’s remaining 90 ms as roughly its p99.
Pages that still wait on a slow call: 1 − 0.9999^100 ≈ 0.01, about 1%.
Extra load: only calls past the p95, about 5% of them, send a copy, so backends see about 5% more reads.
numbers.result: Hedging at the p95 cuts slow pages from about 63% to about 1% for about 5% more read load, assuming independent slowdowns; correlated slowdowns (a whole zone degrading) shrink the benefit.

india.title: Flight search across many fare sources
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Picture an Indian travel-search site that asks around 40 airline and fare sources for prices on every search. If each source is slow on 2% of calls, 1 − 0.98^40 ≈ 55% of searches would wait for a laggard. A sensible design gives each source a deadline of about 1.5 seconds, shows the fares that have arrived, marks the result as still updating, and fills in late fares as they come. Fare lookups are reads, so a second copy to another endpoint is safe; the booking call that follows is not hedged and carries an idempotency key. These numbers are illustrative, not any company’s real figures.

pitfalls.trap: Hedging every call immediately, which doubles backend load and can tip a busy cluster into overload.
pitfalls.say: Hedge after about the p95, under a budget such as 5% extra requests, and cancel the losing copy.

pitfalls.trap: Assuming two replicas are slow independently when they share a host, a zone or a hot partition.
pitfalls.say: Send the hedge to a replica in a different failure domain, and measure how often both copies are slow.

pitfalls.trap: Hedging writes because the client library makes it a single setting.
pitfalls.say: Restrict hedging to reads and calls with idempotency keys; review it like any retry policy.

takeaways: A fan-out request is as slow as its slowest call: 1 − 0.99^N of requests hit a 1% tail.
Hedge reads after about the p95 and cap the extra load with a budget.
Turn the page budget into per-call deadlines and return marked partial results where the product allows.
Measure p99 and p99.9 per fan-out level; averages hide the tail.

interactive.title: Fan-out from 10 to 100
interactive.prompt: Each backend call is slow 1% of the time, independently. A product page grows from 10 backends to 100. What happens to the share of slow page loads?

choices.label: It rises from about 10% to about 63%
It stays at 1%, because each backend is unchanged
choices.feedback: Each backend is unchanged, but the page now needs all 100 of them to be fast.

choices.label: It rises tenfold, from about 10% to 100%
choices.feedback: The odds compound rather than add: about 37% of pages still have no slow call.

interactive.reveal: Wide fan-out turns a backend’s rare tail into the page’s common case. Cut it with hedged reads after the p95, per-call deadlines and partial results, and watch p99 rather than the average.

seeAlso.why: Timeouts and retries set the deadlines that hedging builds on.
You need p99 latency metrics and traces to see the tail at all.
Hedged calls must be idempotent, which is what idempotency keys provide.

title: Hot Keys and Skewed Partitions
objectives: Explain why one hot key can overload a shard while the cluster is mostly idle
Choose read-side fixes (local caching, key replicas) or write-side fixes (split counters, batching)
Spot shard keys that create skew, such as timestamps or low-cardinality fields

cards.title: Capacity is per shard, not per cluster
cards.body: Hashing spreads keys evenly, but it cannot split a single key: every request for that key lands on one shard. With 10 shards that each handle 10K operations per second, the cluster can do 100K per second in total, yet one key receiving 30K per second overloads its shard while the other nine sit mostly idle. Celebrity profiles, a flash-sale product and the live score of a big match are typical hot keys.

cards.title: Worked example: a like counter on a viral post
cards.body: Assume: 50,000 likes per second on one post at peak; one partition handles about 5,000 counter writes per second comfortably.
steps: One counter key would need 50,000 writes per second on one partition, ten times its comfortable limit.
Split it into sub-counters likes:post42:0 to likes:post42:N−1; each like increments one sub-counter chosen at random.
Minimum N = 50,000 ÷ 5,000 = 10; choose 16 for headroom, so each sub-counter takes about 50,000 ÷ 16 ≈ 3,125 writes per second.
A read fetches all 16 sub-counters in one batched call and sums them; caching the total for one second keeps reads cheap.
cards.note: Splitting turns one hot write key into N ordinary keys; the price is a fan-in on every read, so cache the sum briefly.

cards.title: Read-hot or write-hot decides the fix
cards.body: A read-hot key (a product page read 200K times per second but changed once a minute) is fixed by copying it: a short-TTL cache inside each app server, or several replicas of the key (product:9#0 to #7) that readers pick at random. A write-hot key needs the writes themselves spread or reduced: split counters, or batching increments in memory and flushing every second. Read replicas of the shard do nothing for write-hot keys.

cards.title: Shard keys that create their own hot spot
cards.body: Some keys are skewed by design. Range-sharding on a timestamp or an increasing id sends every new write to the newest shard. Sharding on a low-cardinality field such as country or city puts one large city on one shard. Prefer high-cardinality keys, hash them, and measure per-key load: a Count-Min sketch or sampled top-k per shard finds hot keys without counting every key exactly.

cards.title: Trap: adding shards for a single hot key
cards.body: Doubling the shard count halves the load per shard for ordinary keys, but the hot key still lands on exactly one shard with the same traffic. Find the key first, then cache it, replicate it or split it; more shards only help when the load is spread across many keys.

questions.prompt: A cluster has 10 shards, each good for 10K operations per second. One key gets 30K per second, and the rest of the traffic is light. What happens?

choices.label: The load spreads across the 10 shards by itself
Its one shard overloads, while the others stay idle
Nothing, since 30K is below the 100K total
Consistent hashing moves the key to an idle shard

questions.explanation: A key maps to one shard, so that shard receives all 30K per second. Hashing spreads different keys, not one key; the 100K total is irrelevant; consistent hashing decides placement once, it does not rebalance by load.

questions.prompt: A viral post’s like counter takes 50K writes per second. Which change fixes the write hot spot?

choices.label: Add read replicas to the counter’s shard
Split it into sub-counters and sum them on read
Put a CDN in front of the like button
Raise the cache TTL on the post page

questions.explanation: Sub-counters spread the writes over many keys and shards. Read replicas, a CDN and a longer cache TTL all reduce reads, and this key is hot because of writes.

questions.prompt: A flash-sale product row is read 200K times per second and changes about once a minute. What is the cheapest effective fix?

choices.label: Cache it in each app server for a few seconds
Re-shard the products table on the product id
Split the row into 16 sub-rows that writers update
Move the products table to a bigger database server

questions.explanation: A read-hot, rarely changing key is served from memory close to the app; a few seconds of staleness is acceptable for a product page. Re-sharding still puts the one key on one shard, sub-rows fix write load rather than reads, and a bigger server only raises the ceiling once.

questions.prompt: One post gets 50,000 likes per second. A partition handles at most 5,000 counter writes per second. What is the minimum number of sub-counters?
assumptions: 50,000 increments per second on one logical counter
At most 5,000 writes per second per sub-counter
questions.explanation: Design implication: 10 runs every sub-counter at its limit, so a real design rounds up to 16 or 32, and every read must fetch and sum that many keys.

questions.prompt: Orders are range-sharded on created_at. Why is the newest shard always the busiest?

choices.label: All new orders fall into the latest time range
Older shards are compacted and run faster
Range sharding sends reads to the first shard
Timestamps hash to the same value on each node

questions.explanation: An increasing key puts every insert in the newest range, so one shard takes all writes. Compaction, read routing and hashing do not explain it; range sharding does not hash at all.

questions.prompt: How can each shard find its hottest keys without keeping an exact count for every key?

choices.label: A Bloom filter of the keys seen today
A HyperLogLog of distinct keys per shard
A Count-Min sketch plus a small top-k list
The shard’s average CPU use over one day

questions.explanation: Count-Min estimates per-key frequency in fixed memory, and a top-k list keeps the leaders. A Bloom filter answers membership and HyperLogLog counts distinct keys, neither gives frequency; average CPU shows the shard is busy but not which key.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a split counter.

items.label: Each write increments one random sub-key
Sum them and cache the total briefly
Create N sub-keys for the counter
A read fetches all N sub-keys in one call

questions.explanation: Writes spread across N keys; reads pay a fan-in that the short cache hides.

flashcards.front: Why can one key overload a big cluster?
flashcards.back: Each key lives on one shard; shard capacity, not cluster capacity, limits it.
Short-TTL local caching or several replicas of the key that readers pick at random.
Split it into N sub-counters, write to one at random, sum on read.

sources.title: Amazon DynamoDB docs: designing partition keys to distribute workload
Google Cloud Firestore docs: distributed counters

mechanism.title: How a hot key is found and spread
steps: Each request for a key is routed by the shard map to one partition. Even, hashed placement of keys says nothing about how requests are spread: one key can draw a large share of all traffic.
Per-shard metrics show one shard at its limit while the others are quiet. Per-key sampling, a Count-Min sketch or a top-k list on each shard names the culprit keys.
Classify each hot key. Read-hot keys change rarely but are read constantly; write-hot keys take many updates per second; a few are both.
Read-hot keys are copied: a local in-process cache with a TTL of a few seconds, or K replicas of the value under suffixed keys spread across shards, with readers choosing one at random.
Write-hot keys are split or batched: N sub-counters chosen at random per write, or increments buffered in memory and flushed as one write per second. Reads then fan in over the sub-keys.

Keys that must stay strictly ordered, such as one seat’s state, cannot be split; they get a single owner with a queue in front and admission control, so excess demand waits or is rejected instead of overloading the shard.

useWhen: Counters, leaderboards and live polls that one event can make suddenly popular.
Product, profile or match pages that millions read while they change rarely.
Any sharded store whose per-shard metrics show one partition far above the rest.
avoidWhen: Do not split a key whose updates must be strictly ordered or checked against one value, such as the last unit of stock; use a single owner and admission control instead.
Do not add sub-keys to every counter in advance; most keys are cold and the read fan-in is wasted. Split the keys that measurement shows are hot.

rows: Local cache with a short TTL
Reads fan in over N keys
Up to one flush interval of lag

numbers.title: Sizing a split counter for a live poll
assumptions: 40,000 votes per second on one poll at the peak
One partition handles about 5,000 writes per second comfortably
Results may be about 2 seconds stale
steps: A single key would need 40,000 writes per second on one partition: 8 times its comfortable rate.
Minimum sub-counters: 40,000 ÷ 5,000 = 8; use 16 for headroom, about 2,500 writes per second each.
Reading the total means summing 16 keys; doing that in one batched read every 2 seconds and caching the sum costs about 8 key reads per second.
Alternatively, each of 20 app servers buffers votes and flushes once a second: 20 writes per second reach the store, at up to 1 second of lag.
numbers.result: Either 16 sub-counters or per-server batching brings a 40,000-per-second hot key under one partition’s limit; batching writes far less but loses up to a second of votes if a server crashes before flushing.

india.title: A live poll during a cricket final
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Imagine a streaming app in India running a “who will win?” poll during the last overs of a cricket final. Votes arrive in bursts after every boundary and could reach tens of thousands per second on one poll id, while every other key in the system is quiet. The poll counter is write-hot, so it is split into sub-counters or batched per server; the poll result shown to viewers is read-hot, so it is cached for a couple of seconds at the edge. The numbers here are illustrative, not reported figures from any platform.

pitfalls.trap: Adding shards or nodes when one key is the problem.
pitfalls.say: Check per-key load first; a single key stays on one shard however many shards you add.

pitfalls.trap: Splitting a counter and then reading all sub-keys on every page view.
pitfalls.say: Cache the summed total for a second or two, or maintain it with a background job.

pitfalls.trap: Choosing a timestamp or a city as the shard key.
pitfalls.say: Prefer high-cardinality, hashed keys; if time-ordering matters, prefix the time with a hashed bucket.

takeaways: Capacity is per shard: one key cannot use more than its shard’s capacity.
Read-hot keys are copied (local caches, key replicas); write-hot keys are split or batched.
Unsplittable keys need a single owner, a queue and admission control.
Detect hot keys with per-key sampling or a Count-Min sketch rather than guessing.

interactive.title: A hot poll counter
interactive.prompt: A live poll gets 40,000 votes per second on one key; one partition handles 5,000 writes per second, and results may be 2 seconds stale. Which fix fits?

choices.label: Split the counter into 16 sub-counters and cache the summed total
choices.feedback: Right: writes spread over 16 keys, and the 2-second cache makes reading the total cheap.

choices.label: Add read replicas to the partition that holds the counter
choices.feedback: Replicas copy reads; every vote is still a write to the one primary.

choices.label: Move the counter to the largest available server
choices.feedback: A bigger box buys perhaps 2–4× headroom, not the 8× this key needs.

interactive.reveal: Ask whether a hot key is hot because of reads or writes. Reads are fixed by copying the value; writes by splitting or batching it. Neither is fixed by adding shards.
setup: 40,000 votes per second on one poll id
One partition: about 5,000 writes per second

seeAlso.why: Hot keys are the failure mode that a good shard key alone cannot prevent.
The Distributed Counter boss puts split counters into a full design.
Count-Min sketches find heavy hitters in small, fixed memory.
A hot key that expires can cause a cache stampede on its shard.

title: Event Sourcing and CQRS
objectives: Store state as an append-only log of events and rebuild it by replaying them
Separate the write model from read models (CQRS) and handle their lag
Use snapshots, event versioning and projection rebuilds, and know when the pattern is not worth it

cards.title: Facts first, state second
cards.body: In event sourcing the system of record is an append-only list of facts: WalletCreated, MoneyAdded ₹500, MoneySpent ₹120. The current balance is not stored as the truth; it is computed by replaying the wallet’s events in order. Nothing is updated in place, so the log answers both “what is the balance?” and “how did it get there?”

cards.title: A command becomes an event
cards.body: The write side loads the entity’s state, checks the business rule, appends a new event, and lets projectors update the read models afterwards.
steps: Command arrives: spend ₹120 from wallet 77
Load the latest snapshot and replay newer events
Check the rule: balance must cover ₹120
Append MoneySpent ₹120 with the next sequence number
Projectors update the balance view and the statement view

cards.title: CQRS: one model writes, others serve reads
cards.body: Command Query Responsibility Segregation splits the model that validates and records changes from the models that answer queries. Each read model (current balance, monthly statement, fraud features) is a projection built from the events and stored in whatever shape its queries need. Projections update asynchronously, so a read can lag a write by milliseconds to seconds; show the user the result returned by the command, or read from the write side, when they must see their own change.

cards.title: Worked example: snapshots and rebuilds
cards.body: Assume: a busy wallet records 10 events a day; the platform holds 1 billion events in total and a projector processes 50,000 events per second.
steps: After a year the wallet has about 10 × 365 = 3,650 events; loading it by full replay reads all of them.
With a snapshot every 500 events, a load reads one snapshot plus at most 499 newer events, about 250 on average.
Rebuilding a new or fixed projection replays every event: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 50,000 = 20,000 seconds, about 5.6 hours.
Running the rebuild into a new table and switching reads when it catches up keeps the old view serving meanwhile.
cards.note: Snapshots bound load time; rebuild time grows with total history, so plan rebuilds in hours and run projectors in parallel by partition.

cards.title: Trap: event sourcing for plain CRUD
cards.body: Event sourcing adds versioned event schemas, projections, rebuilds, eventual consistency and harder deletion of personal data (often handled by encrypting each person’s data with their own key and deleting the key). It pays off where history and audit are the product, such as ledgers, orders and workflows; for a settings page or a simple catalogue, a normal table with an audit log is enough.

questions.prompt: In an event-sourced wallet, what is the source of truth?

choices.label: The current-balance read model
The append-only log of wallet events
The cache of balances kept in Redis
The nightly snapshot of each wallet

questions.explanation: The events are the record; everything else is derived. The balance view and the cache are projections that can be rebuilt, and snapshots are a speed-up that can be recomputed from the log.

questions.prompt: What does CQRS separate?

choices.label: Writes in one region from reads in another
Write handling from read-optimised views
Database queries from the cache in front of them
Synchronous APIs from background jobs

questions.explanation: CQRS splits the model that validates commands from the models that serve queries. Regions, caches and background jobs are separate concerns that can exist with or without it.

questions.prompt: A user changes their address and, a second later, the profile page still shows the old one. The system uses CQRS. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The event was lost and must be replayed by hand
The command was rejected by the write model
The read model is updated asynchronously from events
Event sourcing keeps only the first version of a field

questions.explanation: Projections apply events after the write commits, so reads can lag briefly. A lost event or a rejected command would not fix itself a moment later, and event sourcing keeps every version.

questions.prompt: A projection must be rebuilt from 1 billion events at 50,000 events per second. How many hours does the rebuild take?
assumptions: One projector at 50,000 events per second
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about a working day, so rebuilds must run alongside the live view and switch over when caught up; partitioning the replay by wallet across 8 projectors brings it under an hour.

questions.prompt: Loading an account replays 40,000 events and is slow. What is the standard fix?

choices.label: Delete events older than 30 days to shorten replay
Load a periodic snapshot, then replay newer events
Store only the current balance and drop the events
Replay the events in parallel in random order

questions.explanation: A snapshot every few hundred events bounds the replay. Deleting events or keeping only the balance destroys the record the pattern exists for, and events for one entity must be applied in order.

questions.prompt: Which system is the weakest fit for event sourcing?

choices.label: A wallet that must explain each balance change
An order workflow audited by regulators
An admin page for editing office addresses
A trading engine replayed to debug incidents

questions.explanation: Office addresses need current values, not a replayable history, so a table plus an audit log is simpler. The wallet, the audited workflow and the trading engine all need their history.

questions.prompt: Order handling a “spend ₹120” command in an event-sourced wallet.

items.label: Append the MoneySpent event
Load the snapshot and newer events
Projectors update the read models
Receive the command
Check the balance covers ₹120

questions.explanation: Validation happens against current state before the append; read models follow the log.

questions.prompt: An event’s schema must change after a year of history. What is the usual approach?

choices.label: Rewrite the stored events in place to the new shape
Version the event and upcast old versions on read
Remove the old events once the new code ships
Start a fresh log and stop reading the old one

questions.explanation: Stored events are immutable facts, so new code reads old versions through an upcaster. Rewriting or removing history breaks the audit trail, and abandoning the old log loses the state it built.

flashcards.back: Store the facts as an append-only log; compute current state by replaying them.
A read model built from the events, shaped for one kind of query, rebuildable from the log.
They bound how many events must be replayed to load one entity.

mechanism.title: How an event-sourced service handles writes and reads
steps: Each entity (a wallet, an order) has its own ordered stream of events, stored in an append-only table or log keyed by entity id and sequence number.
A command loads the entity by reading its latest snapshot and replaying the events after it, then checks business rules against that state.

If the rule passes, the service appends the new event with the expected next sequence number. A unique constraint on (entity id, sequence) makes two concurrent writers conflict, so one retries: this is optimistic concurrency on the stream.

Projectors read the log in order and update read models: a balance table, a statement table, a search index. Each projector records the last position it applied, so it can restart without double-applying.
Read requests go to the projections. Because projectors run after the append, reads can lag; the command’s response carries the new state for the user who made the change.
Schema changes are handled by versioned events and upcasters. New projections, or fixed ones, are built by replaying the log from the start into a new table, then switching reads.

useWhen: Domains where history is the product: ledgers, orders, claims, workflows that auditors or customers ask about.
Systems that need several very different read shapes from the same writes, such as a balance, a statement and fraud features.
Teams that expect to add new reports or fix projection bugs by replaying the past.
avoidWhen: Simple CRUD screens where only the current value matters; a table with an audit log is cheaper to build and run.
Teams without the operational maturity for replays, schema versioning and eventual consistency between writes and reads.
Data with strict deletion rules unless you design for it, for example per-person encryption keys that can be destroyed.

numbers.title: Snapshot interval and rebuild time
assumptions: A busy wallet: 10 events a day
Total history: 1 billion events
One projector: 50,000 events per second
steps: Events per busy wallet after a year: 10 × 365 = 3,650.
With snapshots every 500 events, a load replays at most 499 events, about 250 on average.
Full rebuild with one projector: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 50,000 = 20,000 seconds, about 5.6 hours.
Partitioned by wallet id over 8 projectors: 20,000 ÷ 8 = 2,500 seconds, about 42 minutes.
numbers.result: Snapshots keep loads to a few hundred events; rebuild time scales with total history, so partition projectors and rebuild into a new table while the old one serves.

india.title: A prepaid wallet’s statements
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Consider an Indian prepaid wallet where customers top up through UPI and pay merchants. Support teams are constantly asked “why is my balance ₹380?”. With event sourcing, each top-up, payment, refund and cashback is an event, and the statement screen is simply a projection of them. When a cashback rule was misapplied for three weeks in this illustrative scenario, the team fixed the projector and rebuilt the affected wallets’ views from the log, while the reversing events themselves went through the normal command path. No real company figures are used here.

pitfalls.trap: Using events as a message bus between services and calling it event sourcing.
pitfalls.say: Event sourcing is about how one service stores its own state; publishing integration events is a separate concern.

pitfalls.trap: Letting read models be the place where business rules are checked.
pitfalls.say: Validate commands against the write model built from the stream; read models may lag.

pitfalls.trap: Changing old events to match new code.
pitfalls.say: Version events and upcast on read; never edit history.

takeaways: The event log is the source of truth; state and read models are derived from it.
CQRS gives each query its own projection, at the cost of read lag after writes.
Snapshots bound load time; rebuilds replay history and are planned in hours.
Use it where history matters; prefer plain tables for simple CRUD.

interactive.title: A projection bug from three months ago
interactive.prompt: A bug in the “monthly spend” projection produced wrong totals for three months. The service is event-sourced. What can you do?

choices.label: Fix the projector and rebuild the view by replaying the events
choices.feedback: Right: the facts were stored correctly; only the derived view was wrong.

choices.label: Nothing: the wrong totals are now permanent
choices.feedback: The view is derived, so it can be recomputed from the log.

choices.label: Edit the stored events so they match the right totals
choices.feedback: The events are correct and immutable; editing them would corrupt the record.

interactive.reveal: Because the log keeps every fact, derived views are disposable: fix the code and replay into a new table, then switch reads. Business corrections, unlike projection bugs, are new events.

seeAlso.why: The outbox pattern and CDC publish events reliably from a database write.
Kafka is a common log for projectors to read, though the event store itself needs per-entity ordering.
Double-entry ledgers share the idea of immutable entries with corrections as new entries.

title: Double-Entry Ledgers and Reconciliation
objectives: Record money movements as balanced, immutable entries and derive balances from them
Store amounts in integer minor units and correct mistakes with reversing entries
Reconcile the internal ledger against bank and payment-provider statements

cards.title: Every movement has two sides
cards.body: In a double-entry ledger a transfer is one transaction with at least two entries that sum to zero: ₹500 debited from Asha’s wallet account and ₹500 credited to Ravi’s. Money is never created or lost inside the system, so the invariant “entries in each transaction sum to zero” catches whole classes of bugs. Balances are the sum of an account’s entries, not a number overwritten in place.

cards.title: Integers, immutability and idempotency
cards.body: Store amounts as integers in the smallest unit (paise), so ₹1,234.56 is 123456. Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly and sums drift. Posted entries are never edited or removed: a mistake is fixed with a reversing entry plus a correct one, which keeps the audit trail. Each transaction carries an idempotency key, so a retried request cannot post twice.

cards.title: Posting one payment
cards.body: A payment is checked for duplicates, written as balanced entries in one database transaction, and matched against the provider’s settlement file later.
steps: Receive the request with an idempotency key
Check the key has not been used
Write the debit and credit entries in one transaction
Commit and return the transaction id
Later, match it against the settlement file

cards.title: Worked example: how many breaks a day?
cards.body: Assume: 2,000,000 transactions a day; automatic matching against bank and provider files pairs 99.9% of them.
steps: Unmatched items per day = 2,000,000 × 0.001 = 2,000.
If a person needs about 3 minutes per item, that is 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 minutes, about 100 hours of work a day.
Adding rules for the common causes (settlement arriving the next day, fees netted from payouts, refunds) lifts matching to 99.99%, leaving 200 items.
200 items at 3 minutes is 10 hours a day: still a small team, so the remaining breaks are grouped by cause and aged.
cards.note: Reconciliation is a product, not a script: track the match rate, the count of open breaks and their age every day.

cards.title: Trap: a balance column as the only record
cards.body: Keeping only UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance − 500 leaves no explanation of how a balance arose, and a lost or doubled update is invisible. Keep the entries as the record; a cached balance is fine if it is updated in the same transaction as the entries and periodically checked against their sum.

questions.prompt: How does a double-entry ledger record a ₹500 transfer from Asha’s wallet to Ravi’s?

choices.label: One row that lowers Asha’s balance column
A debit of 500 to Asha and a credit of 500 to Ravi
Two balance updates in separate transactions
A credit to Ravi, with Asha’s side implied

questions.explanation: Both sides are written in one transaction and sum to zero. A single balance update loses the other side, separate transactions can leave money half-moved, and an implied side cannot be checked.

questions.prompt: Why store money as integer paise rather than floating-point rupees?

choices.label: Integers take less storage space than floats
Floats cannot hold amounts above ₹1 crore
Binary floats cannot represent 0.1 exactly
Databases cannot index floating-point columns

questions.explanation: Values like 0.1 become approximations, so sums of many payments drift by fractions of a paisa. Storage size is similar, floats hold huge values (imprecisely), and floating-point columns can be indexed.

questions.prompt: A posted ledger entry used the wrong amount. How should it be corrected?

choices.label: Update the amount on the original entry
Post a reversing entry, then a correct one
Remove the entry and post a fresh one
Adjust the account’s cached balance directly

questions.explanation: Entries are immutable; a reversal plus a correct entry fixes the balance and keeps the history. Editing or removing the original hides what happened, and adjusting the cached balance breaks its link to the entries.

questions.prompt: What does daily reconciliation compare?

choices.label: The internal ledger against settlement files
Today’s balances against yesterday’s balances
The primary database against its read replica
API logs against load balancer access logs

questions.explanation: Reconciliation checks your record of money against an external record (bank statements, payment-provider settlement files). The other comparisons check internal consistency or traffic, not money.

questions.prompt: A platform processes 2 million transactions a day and automatically matches 99.9% of them. How many unmatched items appear per day?
assumptions: 2,000,000 transactions a day
0.1% are left unmatched
questions.explanation: Design implication: at a few minutes each that is about 100 hours of manual work a day, so the team invests in matching rules until breaks drop to a level people can clear.

questions.prompt: Which automated check catches a bug that created money from nothing?

choices.label: Entries in each transaction sum to zero
No account balance is below zero
Each payment API call returns HTTP 200
Transactions per second stay under the limit

questions.explanation: Created money shows up as a transaction whose entries do not net to zero. A non-negative balance check only fires when a balance drops below zero, so it cannot see money that appears; status codes and throughput say nothing about amounts.

questions.prompt: Order posting a payment to the ledger.

items.label: Write both entries in one transaction
Match it against the settlement file later
Receive the request with an idempotency key
Commit and return the transaction id
Check the key has not been used

questions.explanation: The duplicate check comes before the write, both entries commit together, and reconciliation happens after settlement.

flashcards.back: Entries in every transaction sum to zero; money moves, it is never created inside the system.
With a reversing entry plus a correct entry; posted entries are never edited.
An internal or external record with no matching counterpart, queued for investigation.

sources.title: Martin Fowler: Accounting Patterns (Account, Entry, Transaction)
PostgreSQL docs: numeric and integer types

mechanism.title: How a ledger records and checks money
steps: Accounts represent every place money can sit: each customer wallet, the merchant payable, fees earned, cash held at each bank, money in transit.

A business event (a payment, a refund, a payout) becomes one transaction with two or more entries whose amounts, in integer paise, sum to zero. All entries commit together in one database transaction.
An idempotency key on the transaction makes retries safe: the second attempt finds the key and returns the first result instead of posting again.
Balances are derived as the sum of an account’s entries. For speed, a balance row can be updated in the same transaction and checked against the entry sum by a nightly job.
Mistakes are corrected with new entries: a reversal of the wrong one and a correct one. The history therefore explains every balance at every point in time.
Each day, settlement files from banks and payment providers are matched against ledger entries by reference, amount and date. Unmatched items become breaks with a cause, an owner and an age.

useWhen: Wallets, payment platforms, marketplaces holding money for sellers, and anything that pays out or settles.
Systems that auditors, regulators or customers question line by line.
Any service where a doubled or lost update would mean real money gained or lost.
avoidWhen: A loyalty-points counter with no cash value can use a simpler counter with an audit log.
Do not build a home-made ledger for a team’s first month of a product if a provider’s ledger service already meets the need; adopt the model, not necessarily your own implementation.

rows: Partly, if the log is complete

numbers.title: Sizing reconciliation work
assumptions: 2,000,000 transactions a day
Automatic match rate 99.9%, improved to 99.99% with rules
About 3 minutes of human time per break
steps: Human time: 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 minutes, about 100 hours a day.
Human time: 200 × 3 = 600 minutes, about 10 hours a day.
numbers.result: Each extra nine of automatic matching cuts manual reconciliation tenfold, which is why matching rules are engineered and monitored like any other feature.

india.title: A payment aggregator’s daily close
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Picture an Indian payment aggregator collecting UPI and card payments for merchants and paying them out a day later. Its ledger has accounts for each merchant’s payable balance, fees earned, money in transit from each acquiring bank and money held in its nodal or escrow account. Every morning, the bank and network settlement files are matched against yesterday’s entries; common breaks are payments that settle in a later cycle, chargebacks and fee differences. Each break is aged, and anything older than a few days goes to finance. The structure is illustrative; no company’s real volumes are used.

pitfalls.trap: Using floating-point columns for money because the language default is a float.
pitfalls.say: Use integers in paise, or a fixed-precision decimal type, end to end, including in APIs.

pitfalls.trap: Writing the debit and the credit in two separate transactions.
pitfalls.say: Write all entries of one movement in a single database transaction, guarded by the idempotency key.

pitfalls.trap: Treating reconciliation as a one-off script.
pitfalls.say: Run it daily, track match rate and open-break age, and alert when they worsen.

takeaways: Each money movement is a transaction of entries that sum to zero.
Use integer minor units, immutable entries and reversals for corrections.
Idempotency keys stop retries from posting twice.
Daily reconciliation against external records finds what internal checks cannot.

interactive.title: Storing wallet balances
interactive.prompt: Choose how to store balances for a wallet that auditors review and that handles a few thousand payments per second.

choices.label: Balanced ledger entries, with a cached balance updated in the same transaction
choices.feedback: Right: entries explain every balance and the cache keeps reads fast.

choices.label: A balance column, updated in place on each payment
choices.feedback: Fast, but a lost or doubled update leaves no trace to find it.

choices.label: A floating-point balance column for faster arithmetic
choices.feedback: Float rounding drifts over millions of payments, and there is still no history.

interactive.reveal: Make the entries the record and treat any balance as a cache that is checked against them. Reconcile daily against bank and provider files to catch what internal checks miss.
setup: Auditors ask why each balance changed
A few thousand payments per second

seeAlso.why: Both entries of a transfer must commit atomically in one ACID transaction.
Idempotency keys stop a retried payment from posting twice.
Event sourcing applies the same immutable-history idea to any entity, not only money.
The digital wallet case study applies the ledger to a full product.
Money in code: minor units, rounding and currency, the amounts every ledger entry depends on

title: Live Data Migration and Resharding
objectives: Move data to a new store or shard layout without downtime: dual writes or CDC, backfill, verify, cut over
Prevent a backfill from overwriting newer data, and keep a rollback path
Estimate backfill time and how many keys a resharding moves

cards.title: Two stores, one truth at a time
cards.body: A live migration moves data while the application keeps serving. For a while two stores hold the data: the old one remains the source of truth while the new one catches up, and only after it is proven correct do reads, and then writes, switch over. Every step must be reversible until the old store is finally retired.

cards.title: The migration sequence
cards.body: New changes flow to the new store first, then history is copied, then answers are compared, and only then does traffic move.
steps: Start copying new changes (dual writes or CDC)
Backfill existing rows in throttled batches
Compare answers with shadow reads
Move reads over gradually
Make the new store the writer and retire the old one

cards.title: Why changes are captured before the backfill
cards.body: If the backfill runs first, rows updated while it runs are copied in their old state and never fixed. Starting change capture first means every later change reaches the new store. The backfill can then copy an old version of a row after the newer one has arrived, so each write carries a version or updated-at value and the new store keeps the newer one.

cards.title: Worked example: backfill time and keys moved
cards.body: Assume: 2 TB to copy, throttled to 50 MB per second to protect the live database; separately, a hash-sharded table grows from 8 to 16 shards using hash mod N.
steps: Backfill: 2,000,000 MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 40,000 seconds, about 11 hours.
At night the throttle can rise to 150 MB/s, so a run mostly at night finishes in roughly 4 to 6 hours.
Resharding with hash mod N from 8 to 16: a key stays put only if hash mod 16 is below 8, which is half of keys, so about 50% of rows move.
With 256 logical shards mapped onto 8 machines, moving to 16 machines moves whole logical shards: half of them relocate, but no key changes its logical shard.
cards.note: Throttled backfills take hours, so change capture must run the whole time; plan resharding with logical shards so data moves in large, verifiable units.

cards.title: Trap: a big-bang cutover with no way back
cards.body: Switching all reads and writes at once, straight after the backfill, bets everything on an unverified copy. Compare a sample of reads first, move traffic in steps (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%), and keep writing to the old store until the new one has run cleanly for a while, so rollback is a configuration change rather than a restore.

questions.prompt: Order a zero-downtime migration to a new database.

items.label: Compare answers with shadow reads
Start dual writes or CDC to the new store
Stop writing to the old store
Backfill existing rows
Move reads over gradually

questions.explanation: Capture changes first, copy history, verify, move reads, and retire the old writer last.

questions.prompt: Why start dual writes or CDC before the backfill rather than after it?

choices.label: The backfill reads the change stream to find rows
Rows changed during the backfill would be missed
Dual writes make the backfill itself run faster
CDC tools attach only to an empty target table

questions.explanation: Without change capture running, an update to a row the backfill has already copied never reaches the new store. The backfill reads the source table, not the stream; dual writes add load rather than speed; and CDC targets need not be empty.

questions.prompt: The backfill copies an old version of a row after a dual write has already stored a newer one. How do you stop the overwrite?

choices.label: Run the backfill only during the night
Pause dual writes while the backfill runs
Write with a version check so newer wins
Re-run the backfill until row counts match

questions.explanation: A conditional write that keeps the higher version or updated-at makes the order of arrival irrelevant. Night runs reduce but do not remove the race, pausing dual writes loses changes, and row counts match even when contents differ.

questions.prompt: A backfill must copy 2 TB at a throttled 50 MB per second. About how many hours does it take?
assumptions: Steady 50 MB per second
questions.explanation: Sanity check: half a day of copying means change capture and lag monitoring must be running throughout, and the plan needs a pause-and-resume checkpoint.

questions.prompt: What do shadow reads give you before the cutover?

choices.label: Lower read latency for users during the move
Evidence that the new store gives the same answers
A backup of the old store, kept in the new one
A way to skip the backfill for cold rows

questions.explanation: A sample of reads also goes to the new store, and the results are compared and logged, while users still get the old store’s answer. Shadow reads add load rather than cutting latency, they are not a backup, and they do not replace the backfill.

questions.prompt: A table is sharded with hash(key) mod N. N goes from 8 to 16. About what share of keys must move?

choices.label: About 1/16 of keys
About 1/8 of keys
About half of keys
Nearly all keys

questions.explanation: A key keeps its shard only when hash mod 16 equals hash mod 8, which holds for half of all hashes. 1/8 and 1/16 are the small shares consistent hashing moves when one node joins a cluster of about that size; nearly all keys move when N grows by one, for example 8 to 9.

questions.prompt: After reads move to the new store, why keep writing to the old one for a while?

choices.label: So you can switch back if a problem appears
To keep the old store’s caches warm for users
Because CDC needs two live writers to work
So the backfill can finish in the background

questions.explanation: While the old store stays current, rollback is just pointing reads back. Warm caches are a minor side effect, CDC needs one source, and the backfill must finish before reads move.

flashcards.back: Otherwise rows changed during the backfill are copied stale and never fixed.

flashcards.front: What stops a backfill overwriting newer data?
flashcards.back: Versioned or updated-at conditional writes: newer wins.

flashcards.front: hash mod N from 8 to 16 moves how much?
flashcards.back: About half the keys; logical shards avoid re-hashing keys.

sources.title: Stripe engineering: Online migrations at scale
Martin Fowler: Parallel Change (expand and contract)

mechanism.title: How a live migration proceeds
steps: Prepare the new store and schema. Add version or updated-at columns if the source lacks them, so later writes can be compared.
Start capturing changes: either the application writes to both stores (dual writes, old store first and authoritative) or CDC streams the old store’s log to the new one. Monitor the lag.

Backfill existing rows in small batches, ordered by primary key, with a checkpoint so the job can pause and resume. Throttle on the source database’s load, and use conditional writes so a stale copy never replaces a newer change.
Verify: compare row counts and checksums per key range, and send a sample of production reads to both stores (shadow reads), logging mismatches until the rate is zero or explained.
Move reads gradually behind a flag, watching errors and latency at each step. The old store remains the writer and source of truth.
Flip the writer: the new store becomes authoritative, and changes flow back to the old store for a rollback period. Finally retire the old path and remove the dual-write code.

useWhen: Moving to a new database engine, a new schema, or a new shard layout while the service stays online.
Splitting a table out of a monolith’s database into a service’s own store.
Resharding when shards approach their storage or write limits.
avoidWhen: Small tables that can be copied during a short, announced maintenance window; the machinery costs more than the downtime.
Migrations with no way to compare results (no stable keys or versions); add those first, then migrate.

rows: Simple to start, no extra infrastructure
Partial failures leave stores out of sync
CDC from the old store’s log
Captures every change, even from other writers
Needs log access and lag monitoring

numbers.title: How long a 2 TB backfill takes
assumptions: 2 TB of rows to copy
Throttle of 50 MB per second during the day
Change capture runs throughout
steps: Daytime rate: 2,000,000 MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 40,000 seconds, about 11 hours.
At 150 MB/s overnight, the same copy needs 2,000,000 ÷ 150 ≈ 13,300 seconds, about 3.7 hours.
A run that starts in the evening at 50 MB/s for 2 hours copies 7,200 s × 50 MB/s = 360,000 MB (360 GB), leaving 1,640,000 MB for the night.
Overnight at 150 MB/s: 1,640,000 ÷ 150 ≈ 10,900 seconds, about 3 hours, so the backfill completes by early morning.
numbers.result: A throttled 2 TB copy takes about 5 to 11 hours depending on when it runs; plan checkpoints and keep change capture running for the whole time.

india.title: Moving an orders table before the festive season
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Imagine an Indian food-delivery company whose single orders table is nearing its write limit a few months before the festive season. The team adds CDC from the old database to a new sharded store, backfills two years of orders over several nights, and sends 1% of order-history reads to both stores for a week. Shadow reads reveal a timezone bug in delivery timestamps for a small share of rows, which is fixed before any user sees it. Reads then move in steps, and the old store stays in sync for two weeks as a rollback path. The details are illustrative.

pitfalls.trap: Starting the backfill before change capture is running.
pitfalls.say: Start CDC or dual writes first and confirm the lag is small, then backfill.

pitfalls.trap: Trusting row counts as proof the copy is right.
pitfalls.say: Compare checksums per key range and run shadow reads on real queries.

pitfalls.trap: Deleting the old store the day after cutover.
pitfalls.say: Keep it in sync for a rollback period sized to how long problems take to surface.

takeaways: Capture changes first, then backfill with conditional, versioned writes.
Verify with checksums and shadow reads before moving traffic.
Move reads gradually, then the writer, and keep a rollback period.
Backfills take hours; logical shards make resharding a matter of moving whole units.

interactive.title: A bug found after cutover
interactive.prompt: You switched all reads to the new database right after the backfill. A timezone bug in the copy now shows wrong order times on 5% of rows. What would most likely have caught it first?

choices.label: Shadow reads comparing a sample of answers before cutover
choices.feedback: Right: compared answers would have shown the 5% mismatch while users still saw the old store.

choices.label: Matching row counts between the two stores
choices.feedback: Counts match even when values inside the rows are wrong.

choices.label: A faster CDC pipeline with lower lag
choices.feedback: Lag affects freshness; the copy logic itself was wrong.

interactive.reveal: Verification has to compare contents, not totals: checksums per key range and shadow reads on real queries, while the old store is still the one serving users and still receiving writes for rollback.

seeAlso.why: Logical shards make resharding a move of whole units instead of re-hashing keys.
CDC from the outbox or the database log is the usual change-capture path.
Schema changes inside one database use the same expand, backfill and contract steps; this lesson moves data between stores.

title: Cell-Based Architecture and Blast Radius
objectives: Split a system into independent cells that each serve a slice of customers
Estimate the blast radius of a bad deploy or a failing dependency
Use a thin router, per-cell rollouts and shuffle sharding to contain failures

cards.title: A cell is a whole copy of the stack
cards.body: A cell is a complete, independent deployment of the service (load balancer, app servers, database, cache, queues) that serves only a slice of customers. A thin routing layer maps each customer to one cell. A bad deploy, a poison request or an overloaded database then hurts only that cell’s customers, not everyone.

cards.title: Worked example: blast radius with 20 cells
cards.body: Assume: customers are spread evenly over 20 cells; deploys go to one cell first and wait an hour before the next wave.
steps: Each cell serves 100% ÷ 20 = 5% of customers.
A bad configuration that breaks the first cell affects about 5% of customers, for as long as detection and rollback take.
The same change pushed everywhere at once would affect 100%.
Waves of 1, then 3, then 16 cells cap exposure at 5%, then 20%, before the full rollout.
cards.note: The cell size is the blast radius: choose it from how many customers you can afford to hurt during one incident.

cards.title: Request path in a cell architecture
cards.body: The router does a quick lookup and forwards; everything else happens inside one cell.
steps: Request arrives with a customer or merchant id
Router looks up the id’s cell in a small, cached table
Request goes to that cell’s load balancer
The cell’s own services and database handle it
Response returns through the router

cards.title: Keeping the router thin, and growing by adding cells
cards.body: The router is shared by every cell, so it must stay small: a cached customer-to-cell map and forwarding, with no business logic. Each cell has a maximum size that has been load-tested; growth means adding cells, not enlarging them, so the tested limits keep holding. Moving a customer between cells is a planned data migration.

cards.title: Trap: cells that share a dependency
cards.body: Cells that all write to one global database or call one shared service are not isolated; that dependency fails them together. Keep data and critical dependencies inside each cell, and treat the few truly global pieces (the router, identity, billing aggregation) as separately hardened systems. Shuffle sharding reduces the overlap further: give each customer a random pair of workers, so that one bad customer shares both workers with few others. With 10 workers there are 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45 possible pairs, so only about 1 in 45 other customers loses both of its workers; the rest keep at least one.

questions.prompt: In a cell-based architecture, what is a cell?

choices.label: One availability zone of a shared database
A container that runs one microservice
A full copy of the stack for a slice of customers
A cache partition for one group of users

questions.explanation: A cell has its own app tier, data and queues and serves some customers end to end. A zone of a shared database, a single container or a cache partition each isolate only one layer.

questions.prompt: Customers are spread evenly over 25 cells. A bad config reaches one cell. What percentage of customers is affected?
assumptions: 25 cells of equal size
The change reached exactly one cell
questions.explanation: Design implication: the cell count sets the worst case for a contained failure, so a team that can tolerate only 2% exposure needs about 50 cells or smaller first waves.

questions.prompt: Which component in a cell architecture must stay as thin as possible?

choices.label: The database inside each cell
The app tier inside each cell
The customer-to-cell router
The cache inside each cell

questions.explanation: The router sits in front of every cell, so a bug or overload there has an unlimited blast radius. Components inside a cell can be as rich as needed, because a failure there stays in the cell.

questions.prompt: How should a deploy roll out across 20 cells?

choices.label: To all cells together at a quiet hour
To one cell, then to larger waves of cells
To the largest cell first, then the rest
To staging only, then to all cells together

questions.explanation: Waves limit exposure to one cell’s customers while the change proves itself. Deploying everywhere at once, even at a quiet hour or after staging, gives up the containment; starting with the largest cell maximises the first blast radius.

questions.prompt: Traffic doubles over a year. How does a cell architecture usually grow?

choices.label: Add more cells, each kept within its tested size
Double the servers and database size of each cell
Merge the cells into one larger shared pool
Route the extra traffic through the router’s cache

questions.explanation: Adding cells keeps each one inside limits that were load-tested. Doubling each cell’s size moves it into untested territory, merging removes isolation, and the router forwards traffic rather than serving it.

questions.prompt: There are 8 workers, and each customer is assigned 2 at random. A poison customer crashes both of its workers. What share of other customers lose both of theirs?

choices.label: About 1 in 4
About 1 in 8
About 1 in 28
About 1 in 2

questions.explanation: There are 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 possible pairs, and only customers with the same pair lose both workers. 1 in 4 is the share holding one specific worker; about 1 in 2 (13 of 28 pairs) is the share that loses at least one worker but keeps the other; 1 in 8 does not follow from the pairing.

questions.prompt: Order a request through a cell-based system.

items.label: Router looks up the customer’s cell
The cell’s services and database handle it
Request arrives with a customer id
Request goes to that cell’s load balancer

questions.explanation: The only shared step is the router lookup; the work happens inside one cell.

flashcards.back: An independent full stack serving a slice of customers, behind a thin router.
The share of customers in the cells a failure or deploy reaches.
By adding cells of a tested size, not by enlarging existing ones.

mechanism.title: How cells contain failures
steps: Choose a partition key that most requests carry and that rarely needs cross-partition work: a merchant id, a tenant id or a customer id.
Build the cell: a full, independent copy of the service with its own database, cache and queues, sized to a maximum that has been load-tested.
Put a thin router in front: it maps the key to a cell through a small, cached table and forwards the request. It holds no business logic and is deployed and scaled more cautiously than anything else.
Deploy cell by cell: one cell first, then waves of more cells, with automated checks and rollback between waves.
Grow by adding cells. New customers are placed in new cells; existing customers move only through a planned migration of their data.

Handle the global pieces separately: cross-cell reports read from a warehouse fed by every cell, and the few shared services (identity, the router) get extra redundancy because their failure is not contained.

useWhen: Large multi-customer services where one customer’s spike, bad input or a bad deploy must not take everyone down.
Platforms that already partition naturally by merchant, tenant or region.
Teams that want deploy safety stronger than a canary inside one shared fleet.
avoidWhen: Small systems: running many full stacks multiplies cost and operations before there is a blast radius worth containing.
Products dominated by cross-customer features, such as a global social graph, where most requests would span cells.

columns: Blast radius of one bad deploy
rows: Few customers share a bad pair

numbers.title: Choosing a cell count
assumptions: Merchants are spread evenly across cells
An incident takes about 30 minutes to detect and roll back
The business tolerates at most 5% of merchants affected per incident
steps: Blast radius per cell = 100% ÷ cells, so 5% needs at least 100 ÷ 5 = 20 cells.
With 20 cells, one bad deploy affects about 5% of merchants for about 30 minutes.
Merchant-minutes lost: 5% of merchants × 30 minutes = 1.5 minutes per merchant on average, against 30 minutes for every merchant if the change went everywhere at once.
If each cell is load-tested to 10,000 requests per second and peak is 150,000, 150,000 ÷ 10,000 = 15 cells of capacity are needed, so the blast-radius target (20), not load, sets the count.
numbers.result: Pick the number of cells from the larger of the blast-radius target and the capacity need; here containment, not traffic, decides on 20.

india.title: Merchant cells for a payments platform
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Picture an Indian payments company serving hundreds of thousands of merchants. A sale event at one large marketplace merchant, or a merchant integration sending malformed requests, should not slow payments for a neighbourhood pharmacy. Placing merchants into cells by merchant id, with the very largest merchants in cells of their own, keeps such incidents local, and deploys reach one cell before the rest. Settlement reports that span merchants are built from a warehouse fed by every cell. This design is illustrative and does not describe any specific company’s system.

pitfalls.trap: Calling it cells while every cell writes to one shared database.
pitfalls.say: Give each cell its own data and critical dependencies; list the remaining shared parts and harden them.

pitfalls.trap: Putting routing rules, feature logic or retries into the router.
pitfalls.say: Keep the router to a cached lookup and forwarding, and change it rarely and carefully.

pitfalls.trap: Enlarging cells as traffic grows.
pitfalls.say: Keep the tested maximum size and add cells; re-test when the limit itself changes.

takeaways: A cell is an independent full stack serving a slice of customers.
Cell size is blast radius; deploy cell by cell in waves.
Keep the router thin and grow by adding cells.
Shuffle sharding further reduces how many customers share a failure.

interactive.title: A bad config in one cell
interactive.prompt: A bad configuration push reaches one of 20 equally sized cells before the automated check stops the rollout. What do customers see?

choices.label: About 5% are affected; the other 19 cells keep serving
choices.feedback: Right: each cell holds about 1/20 of customers, and the push stopped at one.

choices.label: Everyone is affected, because all cells sit behind one router
choices.feedback: The router only forwards; the bad config lives in one cell’s stack.

choices.label: Nobody, because the router retries the requests in a healthy cell
choices.feedback: Other cells do not hold this cell’s customers’ data, so they cannot serve them.

interactive.reveal: Cells turn a global outage into a partial one whose size you choose in advance. The price is running many stacks, a carefully guarded router and planned migrations when customers move between cells.

seeAlso.why: Availability maths explains why limiting the affected share matters as much as uptime.
Canaries and waves are how changes reach cells one at a time.
Large tenants often get dedicated cells to isolate noisy neighbours.

title: Queueing, Utilisation and Little’s Law
objectives: Use Little’s Law (in flight = arrival rate × time in system) to size pools and concurrency
Explain why waiting time climbs steeply as utilisation approaches 100%
Choose bounded queues and target utilisation instead of running hot

cards.title: Little’s Law: in flight equals rate times time
cards.body: For any stable system, the average number of requests inside it equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each spends there: L = λ × W. A service receiving 2,000 requests per second that each take 50 ms has 2,000 × 0.05 = 100 requests in flight on average. The law needs no assumptions about the traffic’s shape, which makes it the quickest sizing tool you have.

cards.title: Worked example: a slow dependency exhausts a pool
cards.body: Assume: 2,000 requests per second; each holds a worker thread for 50 ms normally; the pool has 200 threads.
steps: Normal: 2,000 × 0.05 = 100 threads busy on average, half the pool.
A dependency slows so each request holds its thread for 150 ms: 2,000 × 0.15 = 300 threads needed.
The pool has only 200, so requests queue for a thread, which adds waiting time, which keeps threads held longer.
Traffic did not change at all; latency alone tripled the concurrency needed.
cards.note: Size pools from rate × holding time with headroom, and put timeouts on slow dependencies so holding time stays bounded.

cards.title: Why 90% busy feels broken
cards.body: Utilisation is arrival rate divided by capacity. With random arrivals, a simple single-server model gives an average queueing delay of about utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation) service times: 1× at 50%, 4× at 80%, 9× at 90% and 19× at 95%. The curve is gentle until about 70% and then bends sharply, which is why capacity plans target roughly 60–70% at peak rather than 95%.

cards.title: Sizing a pool with Little’s Law
cards.body: Measure, multiply, add headroom, and bound the queue in front.
steps: Measure the peak arrival rate
Measure how long each request holds the resource
Multiply them for the average number in use
Add headroom so utilisation stays near 70%
Bound the queue in front of the pool

cards.title: Trap: an unbounded queue as a safety net
cards.body: An unbounded queue does not create capacity; when arrivals exceed service rate it grows until waits pass every client’s timeout, and the server spends its time on requests nobody is waiting for. Bound the queue, reject or shed the excess quickly, and let clients back off.

questions.prompt: A service handles 2,000 requests per second, and each spends 50 ms in the service. On average, how many requests are in flight?
assumptions: Arrival rate 2,000 per second
Time in system 50 ms = 0.05 s
questions.explanation: Sanity check: if the 50 ms is mistakenly used as 50 seconds the answer becomes 100,000, and dividing instead of multiplying gives 40,000; units in seconds keep both mistakes out.

questions.prompt: At a steady 2,000 requests per second, a dependency’s latency rises from 50 ms to 200 ms. What happens to requests in flight?

choices.label: They stay near 100, since arrivals are unchanged
They fall, because each request now waits longer
They rise from about 100 to about 400
They rise from about 100 to about 200

questions.explanation: In flight = 2,000 × 0.2 = 400, four times the 100 before. The rate is unchanged, but time in the system grew fourfold; doubling would need 100 ms.

questions.prompt: With random arrivals and a single server, roughly how long is the average queueing delay at 90% utilisation?

choices.label: About 0.9 service times
About 2 service times
About 9 service times
About 90 service times

questions.explanation: Delay ≈ utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation) = 0.9 ÷ 0.1 = 9 service times. 0.9 confuses delay with utilisation, 2 is the rough figure at about 67%, and 90 is the figure near 99%.

questions.prompt: Why do capacity plans target about 60–70% utilisation at peak rather than 95%?

choices.label: Waiting time climbs steeply near 100% busy
Servers wear out faster above 70% CPU
Cloud providers charge extra above 70% CPU
Metrics agents stop reporting on busy hosts

questions.explanation: Queueing delay grows as utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation), so small bursts at 95% create long queues. Hardware wear, billing and monitoring do not change at 70%.

questions.prompt: Peak load keeps 120 workers busy on average. How large a pool keeps the peak near 70% busy?

choices.label: About 84 workers
About 120 workers
About 170 workers
About 400 workers

questions.explanation: 120 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 171, so about 170 workers. 84 multiplies by 0.7 instead of dividing, 120 runs at 100% busy with long queues at every burst, and 400 sits at 30% busy and wastes capacity.

questions.prompt: Arrivals exceed capacity for ten minutes at a festival-sale peak. What should the queue in front of the service be?

choices.label: Unbounded, so that no request is dropped
Bounded, shedding requests beyond a limit
Sorted so the largest requests run first
Removed, with clients retrying straight away

questions.explanation: A bounded queue keeps waits below client timeouts and turns overload into fast rejections. An unbounded queue serves stale requests, largest-first ordering makes waits worse, and immediate client retries add load.

questions.prompt: Traffic is steady when a downstream dependency slows. Put the chain of effects in order.

items.label: The pool fills and new requests wait for a thread
Retries add load and the backlog grows further
Each request holds its thread longer
Waits pass client timeouts and clients retry
Threads in use rise as rate × holding time

questions.explanation: Latency alone drives the overload: Little’s Law turns longer holding time into more concurrency, and retries turn queueing into extra load. Timeouts and bounded queues break the chain early.

flashcards.back: Average in system = arrival rate × average time in system (L = λW).
About 0.9 ÷ 0.1 = 9 service times; at 50% it is about 1.
Unbounded queues grow past client timeouts, so the server does work nobody waits for.
