mechanism.title: How queues form and how to size for them
steps: Requests arrive at some rate and each needs a resource (a thread, a connection, a CPU core) for some time. Little’s Law says the average number holding or waiting for that resource equals rate × time.

Utilisation is the fraction of capacity in use: arrival rate ÷ (number of servers × service rate per server). Below 100% the system is stable on average, but arrivals are bursty, so queues still form during bursts.

The busier the server, the less spare time it has to drain a burst before the next one, so waiting time grows non-linearly. In the single-server random-arrival model the average wait is utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation) service times.
Pools are therefore sized from Little’s Law with headroom, aiming for around 60–70% busy at peak, and per-call timeouts keep holding times from stretching when dependencies slow down.
In front of each pool sits a bounded queue. When it is full, new work is rejected immediately with a retry-after hint, which keeps latency for admitted work predictable.
Monitoring tracks utilisation, queue length and wait time per pool; a growing queue at constant traffic usually means the time per request rose, not the traffic.

useWhen: Sizing thread pools, connection pools, worker fleets and consumer groups.
Explaining latency spikes during peaks, such as a festival sale, when CPU averages look fine.
Setting admission limits and queue bounds before an event.
avoidWhen: Do not apply the single-server formula as an exact prediction for multi-server or highly bursty systems; use it for the shape of the curve and measure the real one with a load test.
Do not use averages measured over a whole day; size from the peak minute.

numbers.title: Sizing a checkout worker pool
assumptions: Peak 3,000 checkout requests per second
Each holds a worker for 40 ms
Target about 70% busy at peak
steps: Average busy workers = 3,000 × 0.04 = 120.
For 70% utilisation, pool size ≈ 120 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 171, so about 175 workers.

If a payment dependency slows to 120 ms, busy workers become 3,000 × 0.12 = 360, about double the pool. Even a 100 ms timeout leaves 3,000 × 0.1 = 300 busy, so a timeout alone is not enough: a circuit breaker or fallback that fails fast must bring holding time back near 40 ms.
Queue bound: 0.5 seconds of work at 3,000 per second is about 1,500 waiting requests; beyond that, reject quickly.
numbers.result: About 175 workers handle the peak at roughly 70% busy; bounding holding time (timeouts plus a fail-fast circuit breaker) matters as much as the pool size, because holding time drives concurrency.

india.title: A Tatkal-style booking rush
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Railway Tatkal booking in India opens at a fixed time each morning, so demand arrives as a wall rather than a curve. For any booking system facing such a rush, Little’s Law explains why a slow payment step is so damaging: if each booking holds a worker twice as long, twice as many workers are needed at the same arrival rate. Systems built for this shape typically put a bounded waiting room in front, admit users at the rate the booking pool can sustain, and show honest wait estimates. The numbers in this lesson are illustrative, not figures from IRCTC.

pitfalls.trap: Sizing a pool from average daily traffic.
pitfalls.say: Size from the peak minute and a measured holding time, then add headroom.

pitfalls.trap: Raising pool sizes when a dependency slows down.
pitfalls.say: Bound holding time with timeouts first; a bigger pool just moves the queue to the dependency.

pitfalls.trap: Running at 90% or more to save money.
pitfalls.say: Plan for about 60–70% at peak; the saving disappears in timeouts and retries.

takeaways: Little’s Law: in flight = arrival rate × time in system.
Waiting time rises steeply as utilisation nears 100%; target about 60–70% at peak.
Slower dependencies raise concurrency as surely as more traffic does.
Bound every queue and reject quickly when it is full.

interactive.title: When does the pool run out?
interactive.prompt: A service gets 2,000 requests per second and has 200 worker threads. Slide how long each request holds a thread and find where the pool runs out.

control.label: Time each request holds a thread

interactive.takeaway: Busy threads = 2,000 × the holding time in seconds. The 200-thread pool fills at 100 ms, with no change in traffic at all, and queues already bite from about 70 ms (140 threads, 70% busy). Slow dependencies, not just traffic spikes, exhaust pools, so bound holding time with timeouts.

seeAlso.why: Back-of-envelope estimates provide the arrival rates that Little’s Law needs.
Timeouts bound how long a request can hold a thread or connection.
Message queues need the same bound-and-drain thinking when consumers fall behind.
Connection pools are sized with the same rate × holding-time rule.
Load shedding and backpressure are what a bounded queue does when it is full.

title: Multi-Tenancy and Noisy Neighbours
objectives: Compare pooled, schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant designs
Enforce tenant isolation in queries, for example with row-level security
Stop one tenant from starving others with per-tenant limits and dedicated capacity for the largest

cards.title: Three ways to share
cards.body: A multi-tenant service serves many customer organisations (tenants) from one product. Pooled: all tenants share tables, and every row carries a tenant_id; cheapest, weakest isolation. Schema or database per tenant: each tenant’s data is separate; stronger isolation and easier per-tenant restore, but thousands of schemas or databases are harder to migrate and monitor. Many products mix them: pooled for small tenants, dedicated for the largest.

cards.title: Isolation lives in every query
cards.body: In a pooled design, one query that forgets WHERE tenant_id = ? leaks another tenant’s data. Resolve the tenant from the authenticated token, never from a request parameter, and add a database-level guard such as row-level security, which filters rows by the session’s tenant even when application code forgets. Put tenant_id first in indexes so each tenant’s rows are found without scanning others.

cards.title: Worked example: one tenant’s export blocks everyone
cards.body: Assume: a shared pool of 100 workers processes jobs first in, first out; one tenant enqueues 1,000 export jobs of 2 seconds each.
steps: Work ahead of the next tenant’s job: 1,000 × 2 = 2,000 worker-seconds.
Spread over 100 workers: 2,000 ÷ 100 = 20 seconds before anyone else’s job starts.
With a per-tenant cap of 10 concurrent jobs, the exporter uses at most 10 workers and the other 90 stay free for everyone else.
The exporter’s own batch now takes 2,000 ÷ 10 = 200 seconds, which is acceptable for a background export.
cards.note: Per-tenant concurrency caps or fair queuing turn one tenant’s burst into that tenant’s own delay instead of everyone’s.

cards.title: A request in a multi-tenant service
cards.body: The tenant is resolved once, then drives limits, routing and data access.
steps: Authenticate and resolve the tenant from the token
Apply that tenant’s rate limit and quota
Route to the tenant’s pool or dedicated cell
Query with the tenant filter enforced by row-level security
Record usage against the tenant for billing

cards.title: Trap: one shared pool for every size of tenant
cards.body: When a few enterprise tenants generate a large share of load, a single shared pool makes everyone’s latency depend on their batch jobs. Give the largest tenants dedicated pools or cells, keep per-tenant limits for the rest, and track usage by tenant in logs or for the top tenants only, since a tenant_id label on every metric can explode series counts.

questions.prompt: Which tenancy model gives the strongest isolation between tenants?

choices.label: Shared tables with a tenant_id column
One schema per tenant in a shared database
A separate database for each tenant
Shared tables plus tenant ids in cache keys

questions.explanation: A database per tenant separates data, load and restores. A schema per tenant still shares the server’s CPU and memory, and shared tables rely on every query filtering correctly, with or without tenant-prefixed cache keys.

questions.prompt: In a pooled, shared-table design, what most often leaks data between tenants?

choices.label: Two tenants having the same row ids
A query that omits the tenant_id filter
Indexes that cover several tenants’ rows
Using UUIDs instead of integer keys

questions.explanation: A missing filter returns other tenants’ rows; row-level security is the backstop. Duplicate ids, shared indexes and the key type do not expose data when queries are filtered.

questions.prompt: 100 shared workers process jobs first in, first out. One tenant enqueues 1,000 jobs of 2 seconds each. About how many seconds does the next tenant’s job wait?
assumptions: 100 workers
1,000 jobs × 2 s ahead in the queue
Strict first-in, first-out
questions.explanation: Design implication: a 20-second stall for every other tenant from one export is why per-tenant concurrency caps or fair queues sit in front of shared workers.

questions.prompt: One tenant’s bulk export slows every other tenant. What is the best first control?

choices.label: A bigger shared worker pool for all tenants
A per-tenant cap on concurrent jobs
A single global rate limit for the service
Separate databases for all 5,000 tenants

questions.explanation: A per-tenant cap confines the burst to its owner. A bigger pool only raises the burst needed to fill it, a global limit throttles everyone equally, and 5,000 databases is a large change for a scheduling problem.

questions.prompt: One tenant generates 30% of traffic and is growing. What is a common move?

choices.label: Give it a dedicated pool or cell of its own
Rate-limit it to the average tenant’s share
Drop its requests during the daily peak
Shard its data across all other tenants

questions.explanation: Dedicated capacity isolates both directions: its load cannot hurt others, and theirs cannot hurt it. Limiting a paying tenant to the average share or dropping its traffic breaks its service, and spreading its data across others spreads its load too.

questions.prompt: Which control keeps tenants’ rows apart inside the database even if application code forgets a filter?

choices.label: A unique index on the tenant_id column
Row-level security policies on tenant_id
A separate connection pool per region
Foreign keys from orders to the tenants table

questions.explanation: Row-level security filters every query by the session’s tenant. A unique index on tenant_id would allow one row per tenant, connection pools do not filter rows, and foreign keys check references rather than visibility.

questions.prompt: Order the handling of a request in a multi-tenant service.

items.label: Route to the tenant’s pool or cell
Record usage for billing
Resolve the tenant from the token
Query with the tenant filter enforced
Apply the tenant’s rate limit

questions.explanation: Identity first, then limits, routing and filtered data access; usage is recorded at the end.

flashcards.back: Pooled is cheapest but relies on filters; separate databases isolate data and load at higher cost.

flashcards.front: Where should the tenant id come from?
flashcards.back: From the authenticated token, never from a request parameter.
Per-tenant limits or fair queuing, and dedicated capacity for the largest tenants.

sources.title: AWS SaaS Lens: silo, bridge and pool isolation

mechanism.title: How a multi-tenant service isolates tenants
steps: Every request is authenticated, and the tenant is taken from the verified token, so a caller cannot ask for another tenant by changing a parameter.
A tenant directory records each tenant’s tier, limits and placement: which pool, schema, database or cell holds its data.
Admission control applies the tenant’s rate limit and concurrency cap before any expensive work; background jobs go into per-tenant or fair-share queues.
Data access sets the tenant on the database session, and row-level security or equivalent filters every query; indexes lead with tenant_id.
The largest or most regulated tenants are placed on dedicated databases or cells, while thousands of small tenants share pooled resources.
Usage is metered per tenant for billing and capacity planning, through logs or a usage table, keeping per-tenant metric labels for the top tenants only.

useWhen: B2B SaaS products serving many organisations from one codebase.
Platforms with a long tail of small customers and a few very large ones.
Services that sell tiers, where limits and isolation differ by plan.
avoidWhen: A single-customer internal system gains nothing from tenancy machinery.
Do not pool tenants whose contracts or regulators require physical separation or a specific data location; give them dedicated stores.

numbers.title: Who pays for a noisy neighbour
assumptions: 100 shared workers, first in, first out
One tenant submits 1,000 jobs of 2 seconds each
Per-tenant cap of 10 concurrent jobs as the fix
steps: Backlog ahead of the next tenant: 1,000 × 2 = 2,000 worker-seconds.
Wait for every other tenant: 2,000 ÷ 100 = 20 seconds.
With the cap, the exporter holds at most 10 workers, leaving 90 for others, so their wait is near zero.
The exporter’s batch takes 2,000 ÷ 10 = 200 seconds instead of 20: the tenant who created the burst absorbs the delay.
numbers.result: Per-tenant caps move the cost of a burst onto the tenant who caused it: 200 seconds for its own batch instead of 20 seconds for everyone.

india.title: GST invoicing during filing week
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Picture an Indian SaaS product that prepares GST invoices and returns for thousands of small businesses and a handful of large enterprises. Load bunches before the monthly return due dates, when a large enterprise may upload hundreds of thousands of invoices at once while small shops file a few dozen. A pooled design with per-tenant upload limits and fair queues keeps small filers responsive, while the largest enterprises run on dedicated databases and worker pools sized for their peaks. Customers with data-location clauses get stores in the agreed region. The scenario is illustrative.

pitfalls.trap: Taking the tenant id from a header or query parameter.
pitfalls.say: Derive it from the authenticated identity and set it on the database session.

pitfalls.trap: Relying only on application code to add tenant filters.
pitfalls.say: Add row-level security or a query layer that injects the filter, and test for cross-tenant reads.

pitfalls.trap: Adding tenant_id as a label on every metric.
pitfalls.say: Meter usage through logs or a usage table, and label metrics for the top tenants only.

takeaways: Choose pooled, schema or database per tenant by isolation needs and tenant size; mix them by tier.
Resolve the tenant from the token and enforce filters in the database.
Per-tenant limits and fair queues make each burst its owner’s problem.
Give the largest tenants dedicated pools or cells.

interactive.title: Tenancy for an invoicing SaaS
interactive.prompt: Choose a data layout for these tenants.

choices.label: Pooled tables for small tenants and dedicated databases for the three enterprises
choices.feedback: Right: cheap for the long tail, isolated and region-pinned for the large contracts.

choices.label: A separate database for each of the 5,003 tenants
choices.feedback: Strong isolation, but thousands of databases to migrate and monitor for little gain.

choices.label: One shared pool for everyone, enterprises included
choices.feedback: Enterprise batch loads would slow small shops, and the residency clauses cannot be met.

interactive.reveal: Tenancy is usually a hybrid: pool the long tail behind per-tenant limits and row-level security, and give large or regulated tenants their own databases or cells.
setup: 5,000 small shops, each with little data
The enterprises’ contracts require data in a named region

The tenant must come from authenticated identity, then be checked on every access.
Cells give the largest tenants dedicated, isolated stacks.
